questions.question: Describe how you would make the new site conform to WCAG 2.2 Level AA, and how accessibility would be checked before each release.
questions.section: B. Website on AEM Sites with Edge Delivery Services
questions.kb:
Our approach
- Your templates are tested against WCAG 2.2 Level AA before launch, and each release is checked the same way, with a record of the results.

How we would do it
- Agree WCAG 2.2 Level AA as the target with your team, then audit your current templates and a sample of pages and record each gap.
- Build each component and template to meet every Level A and AA success criterion, including visible focus, target size, color contrast, headings, form labels and text alternatives.
- Test every template with an automated scan, keyboard-only use and screen readers such as NVDA, JAWS and VoiceOver, and log each issue against its WCAG success criterion.
- Train your authors to write alternative text, headings, link text and table headers, with a checklist to run before they publish each page.
- Set a release gate: each release passes an automated scan and a manual keyboard and screen reader check of changed templates, with no new A or AA failures.

What you get
- Accessibility audit of templates and sample pages
- WCAG 2.2 AA test plan and release checklist
- Issue log mapped to WCAG success criteria
- Author guide and checklist for accessible content

Timeline and effort

- This runs during the build, once discovery has agreed the scope.

Risk we manage

questions.question: Describe how you would achieve and keep strong Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse scores on the new site.
questions.section: B. Website on AEM Sites with Edge Delivery Services
questions.kb:
Our approach
- In Adobe's Keeping it 100 guidance, the delayed phase of page loading holds third-party tags and other assets that are not material to the experience.
- Your key templates launch at their agreed Lighthouse scores, every later release is tested against them, and real visitor data shows any page that slips.

How we would do it
- Measure your current site's Core Web Vitals and Lighthouse scores for each key template, on mobile and desktop, as the baseline we compare against after launch.
- Agree a Lighthouse score per key template for release tests, and Google's good thresholds for real visitors: LCP 2.5 seconds, INP 200 milliseconds and CLS 0.1, at the 75th percentile.
- Build each template so what the first screen needs loads first and third-party tags load last, and check that the CDN caches pages, code and images.
- Test every release against the agreed Lighthouse score before it goes live, and hold any change that drops a key template below its target until it is fixed.
- Track real visitors' Core Web Vitals after launch against the agreed thresholds and the baseline, find the pages and elements that slow them down, and fix the worst first.

What you get
- Baseline and target scores for each key template
- Third-party tag inventory with a load plan
- A performance test in every release
- Post-launch Core Web Vitals report

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: about 24 to 96 hours for this work.

Risk we manage
- Third-party tags added after launch slowing pages again: we agree with your tag owners that each new tag passes the same release test, and watch real visitor data.

- Run load, caching, purge, redirect and page speed tests on stage, then switch your CDN's origin, or DNS where the hostname changes, and hand your CDN team a runbook.

- Load, caching, purge and page speed test results
- Security settings record signed off by your team
- Cutover plan and CDN runbook

questions.question: We will not license Adobe Target in this phase. Describe how you would run A/B tests on the new quote-start page without it.
questions.section: B. Website on AEM Sites with Edge Delivery Services
questions.kb:
Our approach
- You told us: You will not license Adobe Target in this phase.
- Each A/B test on your pages runs to an agreed plan, with each visitor's variant in your analytics, and you keep only the changes the results support.

How we would do it
- Agree a test plan with your team for each test: the hypothesis, one primary metric such as form starts, guardrail metrics, the sample size and the run time.
- Build the challenger as a copy of the control page that changes one thing, such as the headline or call to action, and keep it out of search indexes.
- Send the experiment ID and the variant each visitor sees into your analytics data with every page view and conversion, so each result can be split by variant.
- Check each variant before launch: preview both pages, confirm the tracking records the right variant, start with an even traffic split, and check the split again once real traffic arrives.
- Decide each test at its planned sample size from the primary metric's lift and confidence by variant, then publish the winner as the page and log the learning.

What you get
- Test plan with hypothesis, metrics and sample size
- Challenger pages, kept out of search indexes
- Experiment and variant tracking in your analytics
- Results readout and learnings log for each test

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: about 20 to 80 hours a month.
- This runs every month from the month after launch.

Risk we manage
- Calling a winner too early on too little traffic: we set the sample size and run time before launch, and decide only when the test reaches them.

How we would do it
- Run two discovery workshops with your marketing and product leads to agree customer intents, competitors and the business measures that matter.

- Configure the monitoring portfolio in Brand Visibility from your approved prompt plan, with the agreed markets, languages and competitors, and confirm each pilot user can open the workspace.
- Build Workspace reports for the agreed conversation, recommendation and purchase measures, limited to what the selected data supports.
- Connect and curate the approved content sources for the agreed products, with your reviewers signing off each source.
- Map the agreed banking or insurance discovery questions that Brand Visibility tracks to approved Brand Concierge sources, with an owner for each source.

- Responsibilities for each measure
- Configured monitoring portfolio in Brand Visibility
- Measure definitions
- A live Brand Concierge experience on the agreed pages
- Question-to-source map

Timeline and effort
- Planning estimate: 168 hours.

- Prompts that miss what your customers ask, since AI platforms do not disclose those questions: we build them from agreed intents and your evidence, and your reviewers approve them.

questions.question: Where is AEM Sites as a Cloud Service hosted, and which security certifications does it hold?
questions.catalog:
Where your data is hosted
- AEM Sites: you choose the primary region when the environment is created, for example the US, Canada, the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Japan, Singapore or Australia, as capacity and your entitlements allow. Security certifications and encryption
- AEM Sites: Adobe's Trust Center lists SOC 2 Type 2, SOC 3, ISO 9001, ISO 27001, ISO 27017, ISO 27018, ISO 22301 and CSA STAR Level 2 for Adobe Experience Cloud, which includes these products.⁵,⁶ The list also marks Adobe Experience Cloud GLBA ready, meaning the service can be used in a way that helps you meet your legal obligations for service providers, while you remain responsible for your own compliance.⁵ Data is stored with provider-managed encryption keys by default, and customer-managed keys in Azure Key Vault can be turned on for the program in Cloud Manager.⁷
